project.title: Nature-Based Solutions for Water Management in the Global South: Lessons from Practice
project.description: The project, titled "Rational biological design and transdisciplinary evaluation of constructed wetlands as a sustainable decentralised sanitation solution in Mexico City," is a collaborative initiative led by the University of Glasgow alongside the Metropolitan Autonomous University (UAM), Parakata, and BORDA. Addressing Mexico City's critical sanitation deficit-where only about 42.5% of municipal wastewater is treated-the project targets underserved peri-urban areas, specifically using four constructed wetlands (CWs) in the community of San Mateo Tlaltenango as a primary case study. The primary scientific aim is to optimize the biological performance of these low-cost, low-energy biotechnologies by resolving their operational unpredictability. To achieve this, researchers will conduct extended 12-month field sampling across wet and dry seasons, applying metagenomic sequencing and qPCR analysis to characterize microbial community structures and metabolic functions driving wastewater treatment. Alongside the biological engineering, the project incorporates a transdisciplinary socioeconomic framework to ensure the long-term viability and scalable adoption of decentralized sanitation systems (DSS). The partner organizations will develop a rapid decision-making assessment tool, conduct socio-territorial mapping, and evaluate legal, land-use, and municipal development dimensions across Mexico City. Furthermore, the team will establish sustainable business models, co-management schemes, and training frameworks for local tradespeople, aligning technical solutions with circular economy principles, community needs, and public policy.
